## What this tutorial reproduces

This is the package-based counterpart of
`fiber-seq/code/parsing_functions/extract_m6a_tutorial.rmd`. It reads the same
**31-sample LCL metadata CSV**, full processed tracks in the shared project,
and ALAS1 TSS from the same GENCODE v46 BED. It uses all available full-span
reads at the selected locus; it does not use the small bundled example or cap
the reads per sample.

The first analysis reproduces the original unclustered workflow: a sparse m6A
assay, heatmap, pooled accessibility profile, and matching nucleosome,
FiberHMM TF-footprint and FIRE tracks. An optional second analysis shows
Manhattan/Leiden clusters for exactly the same reads. Both views use public
functions from `selectFiberseqLociWorkflow`; no analysis scripts are sourced.

This tutorial requires access to the shared files. The published HTML includes
its executed output and plots and can be read without that access. For a
portable input dataset, see the package's `example_data()` tutorials.

## 1. Load the installed package and choose settings

Install the package and dependencies using its README before knitting. The
tutorial itself does not install anything. It uses Rsamtools through the
package to read tabix-indexed tracks; an external `tabix` executable is not
needed.

```{r libraries}
library(selectFiberseqLociWorkflow)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(GenomicRanges)
```

Edit the YAML parameters at the top of this Rmd, or supply `params` to
`rmarkdown::render()`. `clustering = FALSE` runs just the original unclustered
analysis. `TRUE` adds a second run and its clustered panels. Bin width,
neighbor count and resolution retain the package defaults below.

```{r settings}
gene <- params$gene
flank_bp <- params$flank_bp
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    setting = c("gene", "flank_bp", "clustering", "window_size",
        "k_neighbors", "resolution", "seed", "nuc_min", "nuc_max",
        "min_tf_score", "smoothing_bp"),
    value = vapply(params[c("gene", "flank_bp", "clustering", "window_size",
        "k_neighbors", "resolution", "seed", "nuc_min", "nuc_max",
        "min_tf_score", "smoothing_bp")], as.character, character(1))))

# With output_dir = NULL, write a new temporary result directory.
# Set output_dir to a new persistent directory when retaining an analysis.
run_dir <- if (is.null(params$output_dir)) {
    tempfile(paste0("LCL-", gene, "-"))
} else {
    path.expand(params$output_dir)
}
if (dir.exists(run_dir) &&
    length(list.files(run_dir, all.files = TRUE, no.. = TRUE))) {
    stop("Choose a new or empty output_dir to avoid replacing an earlier run")
}
dir.create(run_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
run_dir <- normalizePath(run_dir, mustWork = TRUE)
```

`window_size = 0` uses individual observed m6A sites for clustering. A positive
integer, such as `50`, averages calls across observed sites in each occupied
bin of that width in bp. `k_neighbors = 10` requests ten Manhattan nearest
neighbors per read, capped at the number of reads minus one.
`resolution = 1` is the Leiden resolution; larger values generally favor
finer partitions. `smoothing_bp = 10` independently controls profile smoothing.
The stored assay remains at single-base resolution for every bin width.

## 2. Convert the shared sample metadata to a package sample sheet

The original CSV contains many analysis columns. Only `sample_name` and
`fire_dir` are needed here. The sample-sheet order is retained for plotting.
The short sample label comes from the part before the first underscore.

```{r sample-metadata}
if (!file.exists(params$sample_sheet)) {
    stop("Shared sample metadata not found: ", params$sample_sheet)
}
sample_metadata <- read.csv(params$sample_sheet, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(c("sample_name", "fire_dir") %in% names(sample_metadata)))
sample_metadata <- sample_metadata[, c("sample_name", "fire_dir")]
knitr::kable(head(sample_metadata, 3), row.names = FALSE)
```

These are the same four processed track sources used in the original tutorial:

| Track | Location | Declared format |
|:--|:--|:--|
| m6A | `<fire_dir>/extracted_results/m6a_by_chr/<sample>.ft_extracted_m6a.<chr>.bed.gz` | `bed12_fibertools` |
| Nucleosome | `<fire_dir>/extracted_results/nuc_by_chr/<sample>.ft_extracted_nuc.<chr>.bed.gz` | `bed12_fibertools` |
| TF footprint | `<tf_root>/<sample>/<sample>.recalled_tf.bed.gz` | `bed15_fiberhmm_tf` |
| FIRE | `<fire_dir>/additional-outputs-v0.1/fire-peaks/<sample>-v0.1-fire-elements.bed.gz` | `bed11_fire` |

Each file needs its adjacent `.tbi` index. The format is explicit, not guessed
from the caller name or filename. FIRE intervals are joined by read ID; legacy
haplotype tags are not used for grouping. No phased or allele-specific input
is needed.

```{r package-sample-sheet}
samples <- make_sample_sheet(data.frame(
    sample_name = sample_metadata$sample_name,
    sample_label = sub("_.*$", "", sample_metadata$sample_name),
    m6a = file.path(sample_metadata$fire_dir, "extracted_results", "m6a_by_chr",
        "{sample_name}.ft_extracted_m6a.{chr}.bed.gz"),
    m6a_format = "bed12_fibertools",
    nucleosome = file.path(sample_metadata$fire_dir, "extracted_results",
        "nuc_by_chr", "{sample_name}.ft_extracted_nuc.{chr}.bed.gz"),
    nucleosome_format = "bed12_fibertools",
    tf = file.path(params$tf_root, "{sample_name}",
        "{sample_name}.recalled_tf.bed.gz"),
    tf_format = "bed15_fiberhmm_tf",
    fire = file.path(sample_metadata$fire_dir, "additional-outputs-v0.1",
        "fire-peaks", "{sample_name}-v0.1-fire-elements.bed.gz"),
    fire_format = "bed11_fire"),
    output = file.path(run_dir, "samples.tsv"))

knitr::kable(as.data.frame(samples[, c("sample_name", "sample_label")]),
    row.names = FALSE)
```

This render selects **`r nrow(samples)` samples**. Omit an optional track's
path and format columns if that track is unavailable for your dataset. A
supplied but nonexistent file is an input error, so optional tracks should
not be represented by invented paths.

## 3. Prepare the same promoter window

The supplied TSS BED uses one-base BED intervals and names of the form
`geneID;transcriptID;geneName;...`. The package's `gencode_custom` reader
selects the requested gene and expands its TSS. The source file is already
canonical; ordinary GTF/GFF3 annotations are also supported and do not require
canonical transcript tags.

```{r promoter}
region <- prepare_regions(params$tss_bed,
    bed_annotation = "gencode_custom", genes = gene, flank_bp = flank_bp)
if (length(region) != 1L) {
    stop("This single-locus tutorial requires exactly one selected TSS")
}
names(region) <- gene
mcols(region)$region_id <- gene
region <- prepare_regions(region, output = file.path(run_dir, "regions.tsv"))
region
knitr::kable(read.delim(file.path(run_dir, "regions.tsv")), row.names = FALSE)
```

For ALAS1, the original TSS BED is `[52198159, 52198160)` on chr3. With
1,000-bp flanks, the selected BED window is `[52197159, 52199159)` and the R
`GRanges` is **chr3:52197160-52199159**, with TSS **52198160**. BED starts
are converted once; all in-memory coordinates are one-based inclusive.

To analyze PRDX1 instead, set `gene = "PRDX1"`. It is on the minus strand;
the upstream side is to the right on a genomic-coordinate plot. Neither
strand changes the convention that genomic start is less than genomic end.

## 4. Validate and extract the unclustered locus

```{r unclustered-analysis}
validate_inputs(samples, region)
unclustered_results <- analyze_loci(samples, region, clustering = FALSE,
    nuc_min = params$nuc_min, nuc_max = params$nuc_max,
    min_tf_score = params$min_tf_score, smoothing_bp = params$smoothing_bp)
x <- unclustered_results[[gene]]
x
```

The returned assay is a sparse **positions-by-reads** matrix, the transpose
of the original tutorial's read-by-position matrix. The package removes
fibertools sentinel blocks, considers each read's longest overlapping
alignment, and retains it only when it spans the entire window. Reads with
no m6A calls in the window remain in the assay and profile denominators.

```{r qc}
qc <- as.data.frame(metadata(x)$qc)
zero_call <- Matrix::colSums(assay(x, "m6a")) == 0
zero_by_sample <- table(factor(colData(x)$sample_name[zero_call],
    levels = samples$sample_name))
qc$zero_m6a_reads <- as.integer(zero_by_sample[qc$sample_name])
knitr::kable(qc, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(samples_in_sheet = nrow(samples),
    samples_with_full_span_reads = sum(qc$full_span_reads > 0L),
    genomic_bases = nrow(x), full_span_reads = ncol(x),
    zero_m6a_reads = sum(zero_call), m6a_calls = sum(assay(x, "m6a"))))
```

### Keep genomic ranges and read metadata aligned

```{r data-model}
rowRanges(x)[1:3]
colData(x)[1:3, c("sample_name", "original_RID", "start", "end")]
colData(x)$read_range[1:3]
colData(x)$footprints[1]
stopifnot(identical(names(rowRanges(x)), rownames(x)),
    identical(rownames(colData(x)), colnames(x)),
    identical(colData(x)$RID, colnames(x)),
    all(start(colData(x)$read_range) == colData(x)$start),
    all(end(colData(x)$read_range) == colData(x)$end))
```

Each assay column is named `sample_name::original_RID`. `colData$read_range`
contains its alignment as a `GRanges`; `colData$footprints` is a `GRangesList`
with one element per read. Standard experiment subsetting keeps these aligned.
Metadata retain original QC and parameters as run provenance; `locus_profile()`
recomputes fractions for the currently selected columns.

## 5. Unclustered m6A heatmap

Reads are shown vertically in sample-sheet order, then alignment start and
read ID; positions are shown horizontally. Black denotes an observed m6A
call. A zero is an absence of an observed call, not a measurement that every
genomic base is an unmethylated adenine. The sample annotation is farthest
left, followed by the cluster annotation in clustered views. The original
tutorial's coordinate ticks and orange dashed TSS marker are retained.

```{r unclustered-heatmap, fig.height=10}
ComplexHeatmap::draw(plot_locus(x, "heatmap"))
```

## 6. Pooled accessibility profile

Every full-span read, including zero-call reads, contributes to the denominator.
The grey curve shows the fraction at observed positions; the blue curve
is the sliding-window mean. The dashed line marks the supplied TSS.

```{r unclustered-profile, fig.height=4}
profile <- locus_profile(x)
head(profile)
stopifnot(all(profile$cov == ncol(x)))
plot_locus(x, "profile")
```

`locus_profile()` uses observed-call positions, as in the original tutorial.
An all-zero locus returns zero fractions at all bases; a locus with no
full-span reads returns `NA` fractions.

## 7. Matching footprint and FIRE tracks

The same retained reads are used for every panel. Defaults keep nucleosomes
of 130-160 bp inclusive, TF block scores of at least 50, and TF width classes
[10,30), [40,60) and [60,80) bp. Footprint coordinates stay one-based in R;
calls overlapping a locus boundary retain their original interval bounds.

```{r footprint-counts}
footprints <- unlist(colData(x)$footprints, use.names = FALSE)
if (length(footprints)) {
    counts <- as.data.frame(table(track = mcols(footprints)$track,
        class = mcols(footprints)$class))
    knitr::kable(counts[counts$Freq > 0L, ], row.names = FALSE)
}
metadata(x)$empty_footprint_tracks
```

A supplied nucleosome or TF track with no retained calls across the samples
raises `no footprints called in the selected region`. The analysis continues
and records the empty track type. Omitting optional tracks does not raise
this warning.

The figure uses the original 2:6:6 layout: accessibility profile, blue m6A
reads, and overlaid FIRE/nucleosome/TF tracks. FIRE is orange; nucleosomes
are dark blue; the TF classes are purple, magenta and cyan. Read panels have
sample-first annotation strips and matching read order. Genomic intervals
are clipped only for drawing; the stored `GRanges` retain their bounds.

```{r unclustered-footprints, fig.height=14}
plot_locus(x, "footprints")
```

## 8. Optional clustering of the same reads

Set the tutorial parameter `clustering = TRUE` to execute this additional
analysis. It uses the bin size, nearest-neighbor count, resolution and seed
specified at the start. Exact Manhattan distances use memory quadratic in
the number of reads; inspect the locus's read count before applying this to
much larger datasets.

```{r clustered-analysis}
clustered_results <- NULL
clustered_available <- FALSE
if (isTRUE(params$clustering)) {
    clustered_results <- analyze_loci(samples, region, clustering = TRUE,
        window_size = params$window_size, k_neighbors = params$k_neighbors,
        resolution = params$resolution, seed = params$seed,
        nuc_min = params$nuc_min, nuc_max = params$nuc_max,
        min_tf_score = params$min_tf_score, smoothing_bp = params$smoothing_bp)
    clustered <- clustered_results[[gene]]
    stopifnot(identical(assay(x), assay(clustered)),
        identical(colnames(x), colnames(clustered)),
        identical(locus_profile(x), locus_profile(clustered)))
    print(metadata(clustered)$parameters)
    print(metadata(clustered)$clustering_status)
    clustered_available <- "cluster" %in% names(colData(clustered))
    if (clustered_available) {
        print(table(colData(clustered)$sample_label, colData(clustered)$cluster))
        print(head(locus_profile(clustered, by_cluster = TRUE)))
    }
} else {
    cat("Clustering disabled: only the unclustered analysis was run.\n")
}
```

Cluster labels are stored in `colData`; the stored assay and its read order
stay unchanged. Cluster plots order reads by cluster, sample, start and RID,
and profiles use each cluster's own denominator. Clustering requires at least
three reads and two occupied features; otherwise the reason for skipping it
is stored in `metadata`.

Clustered panels use the original Leiden palette throughout. To reuse those
colors in your own plots:

```{r cluster-palette}
if (clustered_available) {
    cluster_colors(colData(clustered)$cluster)
}
```

```{r clustered-heatmap, fig.height=10}
if (clustered_available) {
    ComplexHeatmap::draw(plot_locus(clustered, "heatmap", clustered = TRUE))
}
```

```{r clustered-profile, fig.height=4}
if (clustered_available) {
    print(plot_locus(clustered, "profile", clustered = TRUE))
}
```

```{r clustered-footprints, fig.height=14}
if (clustered_available) {
    print(plot_locus(clustered, "footprints", clustered = TRUE))
}
```

## 9. Export and reload the Bioconductor result

```{r export}
write_locus_results(unclustered_results,
    file.path(run_dir, "without-clustering"))
if (!is.null(clustered_results)) {
    write_locus_results(clustered_results,
        file.path(run_dir, "with-clustering"))
}
list.files(run_dir, recursive = TRUE)

restored <- readRDS(file.path(run_dir, "without-clustering", gene, "locus.rds"))
stopifnot(identical(assay(restored), assay(x)),
    identical(rowRanges(restored), rowRanges(x)),
    identical(colData(restored), colData(x)))
```

Each locus directory contains the complete `locus.rds`, sparse
`m6a_matrix.rds`, read metadata, region table and QC. Its `unclustered/`
directory contains PDF panels, profile/read-order TSVs and a panel manifest.
After successful clustering, `clustered/` contains the corresponding views,
`assignments.tsv` and `edges.tsv`. The clustered run also retains unclustered
views. `samples.tsv` and `regions.tsv` at the run root document the inputs.

For repeat analyses, choose a new output directory. The shared input files
and their indexes are only read.

## Re-run with another locus or clustering settings

Run these commands in R from the directory containing this Rmd. They are shown
without execution so knitting does not start another render recursively.
PRDX1 uses the same 31 sample paths with `{chr}` expanded to chr1.

```r
rmarkdown::render("LCL-fiber-seq-data-example.Rmd",
    output_file = "PRDX1-unclustered.html",
    params = list(gene = "PRDX1", clustering = FALSE,
        output_dir = "../results/PRDX1-unclustered"))

rmarkdown::render("LCL-fiber-seq-data-example.Rmd",
    output_file = "ALAS1-binned-clustering.html",
    params = list(gene = "ALAS1", clustering = TRUE,
        window_size = 50, k_neighbors = 5, resolution = 0.5,
        output_dir = "../results/ALAS1-binned-clustering"))
```

The persistent output directories in these examples must be new or empty.
These paths are relative to the Rmd directory and continue to work after
moving the containing project folder. The shared-data input paths are supplied
through parameters and remain independent of the package checkout location.
